reading.rtitle: The Four Lines That Follow You Everywhere
paras: There is a paragraph that follows you everywhere. It sits under your photo on a festival page, at the top of an email to somebody you have never met, and next to the link to your showreel. It is about four lines long, and most people write it in ten minutes, once, and then never look at it again. Those four lines are the reason a stranger decides whether to open the link, so ten minutes is not enough.

The first mistake is to write a list. I have worked in television since 2016. I have been color grading for seven years. I have three album credits. Each sentence is true, and together they say almost nothing, because a list has no shape. The second mistake is the opposite: a paragraph so general that it could belong to anybody. I have always been passionate about music. Everybody in that room has been passionate about music since they were twelve, and half of them are self-taught as well. Passion is the entry ticket, not the argument.

What works is smaller and stranger. Pick one thing you have specialized in, one room you have run, name the length of time honestly, and then give one detail that only somebody inside the work would know. I have been building backing tracks for live music shows for eight years, and I have learned that the problem is almost never the arrangement. It is that a key that worked in the rehearsal stops working under the lights. A reader who has never met you now knows what you do, and knows that you have actually done it. A milestone deserves one line and never four: you have been nominated for something, or you have delivered a hundred shows, and then you move on.

Two more rules, and both of them are about time. Do not hide the gaps. A year when nothing came out is ordinary, and editing it away only makes the whole timeline look edited. And rewrite the paragraph every six months, because for eight years turns into a lie quietly, while you are not looking. In this industry the work has arrived in a steady trickle by word of mouth since long before any of it was online. Somebody still has to be able to repeat, in one sentence, what it is that you do.

choices: To explain why every producer needs a showreel and a website.
To show what makes a short professional paragraph work, and what makes it fail.
To argue that passion matters more than experience.

items.situation: Say how long you have worked in television, using the moment it started.
tips: I have worked in television since 2016.
Since + the point where it began. A date, a year, an event.

items.situation: Now say the same thing using the length of time instead.
tips: I have worked in television for ten years.
For + how long it has lasted. Never for since 2016.

items.situation: Say what you have specialized in, and add one detail nobody outside the work would know.
tips: I have specialized in backing tracks for live shows, and the real problem is almost never the arrangement.
The detail is the proof. Without it, the sentence is only a claim.

items.situation: Name one milestone in a single line, and then stop.
tips: I have delivered more than a hundred live shows.
One line. Four lines turn a milestone into a complaint.

items.situation: Say that something started in the past and is still running right now.
tips: I have been building the backing tracks for this season since January.
Have been + -ing when the activity is still going on.

items.situation: Now say the whole paragraph about yourself, out loud, in four lines.
tips: One area, the length of time, one inside detail, one milestone.
Say it once, then cut one sentence and say it again.

listenings.text: I have been reading applications for this program for nine years, which means I have read something like four thousand of them, and I can tell you the three things that make me stop. The first one is a number that is specific. Not many years of experience, but I have been doing this since 2016. The moment there is a date, I believe the rest of the paragraph. The second one is a detail from inside the work, the kind of thing you only know if you have been in the room. Somebody wrote to me last year that the hardest part of her job was not the music. It was telling a singer that the key was wrong on the day of the show. I have never forgotten that line. And the third thing is honesty about the gap. Everybody has a year that went quietly. The applications that hide it always look edited, and the ones that name it in six words never do.

Nobody has ever hired me because of my website. I have had one since 2014, I update it about once a year, and as far as I can tell it exists so that people who have already decided to hire me have somewhere to check that I am real. Every single job I have had has arrived the same way: somebody I worked with told somebody else. That is it. Word of mouth, since long before any of this was online. Which means the thing you are actually building is not a showreel. It is a memory in about forty people. And people remember two things about working with you, and neither of them is your best mix. They remember whether you were calm at eleven at night when something broke, and they remember whether you said the difficult thing early, while it could still be fixed. I have been doing this for fifteen years and I have never met an exception.

extra_audio.text: Pedro says he has worked in music and audiovisual production since 2016. He says he has specialized in backing tracks for live music shows. He has delivered more than a hundred shows. He adds that he is self-taught, and that he has been studying songwriting since last year. He mentions that there has been one gap in his timeline, and that he does not hide it. Then he asks the other person how long they have been doing what they do.
